utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Ms. Pilipovic, is the Defence ready to call --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the next witness, Professor Cavoski?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, before that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: On a previous date, the Defence inquired from the Prosecution for the date when the photograph of the Kobilja Glava mosque was taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It was taken in September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This raises another issue. When exactly in September 1992? Because that could be the 1st of September or it could be the 30th. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, at the moment we don't have that information, the exact date. At this present moment, I could only give the month and the year. Perhaps later on in the afternoon I'll be able to inform --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you could provide that information. Would you need the hour and the minutes as well, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, or would the day for the time being be sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think you have understood why we're interested in this matter. I think that today would be sufficient. I'll provide you with the hour, if you need it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Professor Cavoski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that you respond to me in English. Of course, it's up to you whether you want to listen to me in English and to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to testify in English, or whether you'd rather use your own language, because we have --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will speak in Serbo-Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll speak -- as we call it, B/C/S, and you call it Serbo-Croat. The -- would you then please put your headphones on - the usher will assist you - and will you please tell me whether you now receive translation in a language you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration at the beginning of your testimony. The text will be handed out to you now by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor Cavoski. Please be seated. Ms. Pilipovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cavoski, could you please put your headphones on. Mr. Cavoski, good day.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us your full name, your date of birth, in spite of the fact that with your statement you provided a full curriculum.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: My name is Kosta Cavoski. I was born on the 26th of October, 1941 in Banatsko Novo Selo, Pencevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cavoski, could you now tell us what your profession is, not to say what subject you teach at the university.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I'm a professor at the School of Law in Belgrade, and I lecture on the introduction to jurisprudence. I give a course on jurisprudence. In addition to that, I am involved with political philosophy, constitutional law, and national issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that you are interested in constitutional law. Can you tell us for how long this has been the case.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, as a post graduate, I was interested in American federalism. I worked on that subject, and the title of my masters degree was the role of judicial control in shaping American federalism. In the course of my career, I've published three or four books that deal with constitutional law.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Bearing in mind -- Professor, bearing in mind the fact that time is restricted, could you please tell us whether you stand by your written statement which was presented to the Chamber and in which you dealt with the issue of multi-ethnicity in Bosnia and Herzegovina during various historical periods and under various historical circumstances.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes, of course I stand by that statement. And that part of my work, like other work that I have done, was based on my multi-disciplinary research.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, we are particularly interested in the 1990s and from 1990 and onwards, so a period during which it was possible to get an inkling of the events that would lead to the disintegration of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. But we're interested in the constitutional aspect, the aspect of constitutional law with regard to this period. Could you tell us, during this period, just before the conflict in the former Bosnia and Herzegovina broke out, what was the position of Bosnia and Herzegovina in terms of constitutional law?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina was a federative unit of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. At the time the constitution of the SFRJ was in force from 1974. We called it the Brioni constitution and that republic also had a particular constitution of its own in addition to that constitution of the federal unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, as the Republic of BH, which was part of the SFRJ, which laws was it to apply?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: As a federal unit, Bosnia had to apply the federal constitution. The SFRJ constitution and then its own constitution, the federal laws, its own laws, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether the fact that Croatia and Slovenia secede, did that change anything in that regard, when we're talking about applying the federal constitution?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: That didn't change the position of Bosnia and Herzegovina at all because the secession of these two federal units, in terms of constitutional law, it was anti-constitution. It was against the constitution. When this actually happened in the rump Yugoslavia, as we called it at the time, the federal constitution was still applied. Even the money was changed, and this was done on a voluntary basis in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether the constitution was actually enforced in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the constitution of the SFRJ.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, at that time the federal constitution was applied to a certain extent and to a certain extent it wasn't. And at the time there were already attempts to trample on that constitution. One of the attempts consisted of the declaration of the rump assembly of the National Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in which sovereignty was declared or the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This was an act which violated the constitution, the second act which violated the constitution which was also very important was the calling of the referendum on the so-called independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You have now answered our question, but can you tell us when Bosnia and Herzegovina became an independent state?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina gradually became an independent state. It started obtaining international recognition on the 6th of April, 1992. The European Union was the first to recognise it, and this example is then followed by other countries. It achieved this in terms of international law, when it was accepted by the United Nations. In terms of law, after this had been -- after it had been recognised by the United Nations, the state was considered to be independent.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, from the 6th of April, in terms of constitutional law, was there a difference with regard to the implementation of the constitution -- from the 6th of April, to the 27th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Not from the point of view of constitutional law. Bosnia remained a secessionist republic. So in formal terms, it had to respect the federal constitution.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In that legal situation and in accordance with your answer, can you tell us what the position was of the federal army of the former SFRJ in the terms of constitutional law. What was the position of the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army was a constitutional and a legitimate military force before the 6th of April and after the 6th of April. When Bosnia became a member of the UN, then it was of course possible to negotiate on the status of the Yugoslav People's Army. It couldn't be a foreign force, an exterior force in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It couldn't be considered as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said in your answer that through negotiations it was possible to find a solution. Could you perhaps clarify what you mean by "negotiations."

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, the army could have remained. For example, Great Britain still has a basis in Cyprus, and it was a colonial force. And to this very day it has a basis in Cyprus. This happened with other states too. It could also have withdrawn from there. So this was a matter of negotiation between the authorities of the rump Yugoslavia and the authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When I ask you the following question, whether after the withdrawal of the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, is it possible to talk about the implementation of the constitution in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina? I'm talking about the constitution of the SFRJ.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, as soon as the army and police withdraw from given territory, then it's possible to say that the constitution that existed to date is no longer in force, because in addition to the nominal validity of law, its effectiveness is also important. If such effectiveness no longer exists, then it's no longer possible to say for a given order that this order is still in force and still a valid order.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, can you tell us, up until when the constitution of the former federal unit of Bosnia and Herzegovina was in force?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: The constitution up Bosnia and Herzegovina as a federal unit was in force -- remained in force right up until the signing of the Dayton Agreement. So throughout the wartime period, it was necessary to enforce the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And only after all three sides that had signed the Dayton Agreement accepted via an agreement a new constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, only at that point did the constitution that was in force up until then cease to be considered as valid. That happened in Dayton -- or, rather, in Paris, when that agreement was formally signed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that in Bosnia-Herzegovina during that period of time the constitution of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina was implemented, and you say this was the case right up until the Dayton Agreement. Can you tell us how the state functioned after the multi-party elections in the 1990s which were held. Were parts of the constitution changed?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, first of all, there was the amendment number 60 which was introduced. It didn't change anything as far as the constitutionality -- the constituent nature of the peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina was concerned, and this concerned the Croats, the Serbs, and the Muslims. First of all, the constitution was respected, and then later it was respected less and less. So the Muslim side within the common authorities tried to obtain independence. And one of the constituent peoples opposed such independence, and that constituent people, they were the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, before we return to the issue of independence, can you tell us what it means when you talk about the constituent nature of the three peoples.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, it's an expression that we used. It's derived from Latin. The word is derived from Latin. In German they would say "state-forming nature," and that is a better expression, in fact. That means that those three peoples - the Muslims, the Serbs, and the Croats - it means that these three peoples are state-forming peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They form the state. They have a special status contrary to the others who can have the status of an ethnic minority. The Serbs also had the status of a state-forming people, not only in Yugoslavia as a whole but in Serbia, in Croatia, and in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And similarly, the Muslims and the Croats had this status in Serbia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So it's a constituent people that forms the state.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, the organs of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina, did they take any decisions which violated the constitutional order of 1974? And you told us amendment 60.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, first of all, there was the declaration of the rump assembly of the National Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina on so-called sovereignty -- or rather, on independence. And when this decision was taken, it's not only that the representatives of the Serb people did not participate in that. They actually opposed this move. And then after the referendum was held on the so-called independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, after that, a referendum was held. As far as the representatives of the Croatian people is concerned, their position was ambiguous for the simple reason that Croatian deputies followed the interests and the orders that they received from Zagreb. Until Croatian Slovenia were recognised by independent states by the European Union. Until then the Croats in Bosnia supported -- publicly supported the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So they were against the Bosnian Serbs for this reason. When independence obtained international recognition of its -- when Croatia obtained international recognition of its independence, then the Bosnian Croats started conducting their own policies and these policies were in favour of dividing Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you have mentioned the recognition of Croatia. And within that context my question would be as follows: Such non-constitutional decisions of the rump part of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, was this detectable in former statements of the SDA and HDZ parties in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes, of course. When elections were held for the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were certain anti-constitutional activities. For example, Fikret Abdic received the majority of votes, the greatest number of votes in those elections. And then the Party of Democratic Action concluded that instead of him Alija Izetbegovic should be the member of the Presidency and the first president of the Presidency. And then in accordance with the constitution, it was planned that the president of the Presidency should rotate, and Alija Izetbegovic had been the president of the Presidency for five years, although this was prohibited by the constitution. And then in the Croatian part of the presidency was also changed, contrary to the constitution. And when Mr. Koljevic left the Presidency and Mrs. Plavsic, two Serbs were brought into the Presidency, and that was against the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, you mentioned the position of the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the existence of the HDZ in that territory. Can you tell us whether there was a way at the time of joining up the Croats in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And if so, tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes. The Croats in accordance with the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time did something that was allowed. According to the provisions of that constitution, municipalities could form associations if they thought that it was appropriate, necessary. So the Croats in Western Herzegovina and in Central Bosnia formed an association, and this was presented to the public as Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Now that you have answered this question and told us about the constitutional right to form municipal associations by the Croats in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and you said that the name given to this association was Herceg-Bosna, can you tell us whether similar alliances, associations, were formed in other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: The Serbs followed the same route. They formed their own autonomous associations of municipalities in those areas where they were in the majority. So, for example, in Bosnian Krajina there was an association of municipalities which was formed, and then in Eastern Serbian Herzegovina, in Romanija and in that area in the direction of Vlasenica right up to the River Drina, Semberija, too, that was an area where the municipalities formed an association.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that such associations were constitutional. In your opinion, could you consider such associations to be a matter of regionalisation?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, no, according to constitutional theory, regionalisation is a third solution. It's something between real federalism and a unitarian state. It's an order which exists in Italy, in Europe at the moment, and also in Spain, and this is what we call regionalisation. This is a simple association of municipalities within a unitary federal unit -- within a unified federal unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Given your order, could I conclude that it would be wrong to think that the Croats and Serbs in the former Bosnia and Herzegovina embarked on a process of regionalisation?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: No. That answer is completely wrong. It's not a matter of regionalisation in the sense of changing the order of the state. It's a matter of doing something that is allowed by the constitution, and that means it is a matter of forming municipal associations.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of your testimony, you told us how the state organs of Bosnia-Herzegovina functioned after the first multi-party elections. Can you tell us how the authorities, how the government was divided in accordance with the constitution which was in force at the time. And I'm referring to the --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: The three parties that beat the communists at the elections, this was the Party of Democratic Action, then the HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Union, and the SDS, and they formed a government and they divided up the ministries. But very soon after this act of taking over the power, the authorities, they started to have conflicts between them. First of all, because of an announcement of a foreboding that Yugoslavia could fall apart. And of course that's when these anti or unconstitutional acts started to happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, who was -- who was the carrier of the legislative power authority in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: That was the national assembly. That was presided by Momcilo Krajisnik. I think it had 240 members. And then there were two organs. There was the presidency, which consisted of seven members, and the government. The presidency is quite an interesting case because although there were three constitutive peoples, that is, the Muslims, the Serbs, and the Croats, the constitution also said that they should all have two members, two representatives, while the seventh place in the presidency was reserved for a member of other nationalities, that is, ethnic minorities, as we called them. And then it was the most usual to have a Jew as a seventh member because in Sarajevo what happened, that during the reign of Ferdinand of Aragon in Spain, a lot of Jews went over from Spain to Bosnia. So the SDS then elected, or rather, put the candidature of a Jew, and then Ejub Ganic decided that he was going to put himself forward as a Yugoslav. So then Yugoslav found himself as being the seventh number -- as being a Yugoslav. And then after he was elected, he started to then show his real face as a Muslim, which of course became very apparent as he was one of the most extreme ones during the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you told us that the legislature -- legislative body was the national assembly, can you tell us whether the assembly worked in accordance with the constitution that was then in force? We've already elaborated on that.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: To start with it did, but at the very moment when the representatives, that is, the deputies from among the Croatian and the Muslim peoples tried to push through the declaration of sovereignty at its own independence, the president of the assembly, Momcilo Krajisnik, refused to call this session, and so they still called the session without the president. And in a rump constitution, they actually voted through this declaration.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you've told us that this was an unconstitution decision on making this decision on sovereignty independence, were there any other acts that were passed in the national assembly that were offending or violating the then-constitution?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: The key decision was to call a referendum. That was an unconstitutional act.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what was the unconstitutional character of the referendum?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: The valid constitution of the SFRJ did not allow for a secession of any federal unit, not Bosnia-Herzegovina. Particularly, there was an article which provided for that the borders of Yugoslavia could not change without the agreement of all the member units of the federal state. So from the point of view of the valid constitution, the secession was forbidden. So any attempt to have any part of that state secede, that was an unconstitutional act.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, can you tell us whether during this period in 1991 the referendum was also called by the Assembly of the Serb People. And if so, can you tell us, is there a difference between this referendum that you've told us about, called it unconstitutional, and the referendum that was called by the Assembly of the Serb People?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: First of all, this Assembly of the Serb People wasn't a particularly specially selected assembly, but it was made up of previously - from 1990 - elected deputies at perfect legitimate elections. So this assembly was made up of deputies that were at the same time were also deputies of this legitimate National Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And this referendum was then called in order to find out the position of the Serb people with regard to this question. And as the question was do you want to stay within the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, this question from the point of view of the valid constitution was not unconstitutional but the constitution allowed for this kind of question to be put.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, bearing in mind what you've just told us, can you tell us whether you personally know the decisions that were adopted by the National Assembly of the Serb People. Particularly, the decision dated 12th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Because I followed the media and the newspaper meticulously, I remember at that time the assembly -- and it was called of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- it decided on strategic objectives, and it had established some six strategic objectives which the Serb people should follow in the period that was in front of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Telling us that there were six strategic objectives that were adopted, can you tell us if you recall whether one of these objectives was the war option or a war objective.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Serb people, as far as I know, never had war objectives. That is, they never started the war. But they always defended their survival within the existing state, and that is the SFRJ. So if there was war, it was obvious that it was imposed, because somebody in Bosnia -- somebody wanted for Serb people in Bosnia to be moved from their constitutive position of the state-forming people and give them the Serbs, the status of ethnic minority, a subdued ethnic minority. Of course the Serbs opposed this -- oppressed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction: Not subdued. Oppressed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall whether in terms of Sarajevo, regardless of your position, do you know whether in Sarajevo there was a war objective?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, the only thing that the Serbs wanted, they wanted for Bosnia and to start with the Croats and Muslims agreed -- they wanted Bosnia to be divided into three autonomous units, and then on the basis of that in Sarajevo, which at the time had ten municipalities, the division was supposed to take place depending on the ethnic composition of each municipality separately, individually. And since the Serbs had the majority in the border municipalities of Sarajevo, it was natural that those municipalities would be constituting or would be part of the Serb unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, considering you've told us what the objective in terms of Sarajevo -- the city of Sarajevo was and what the situation was. Did you while you were preparing your expert report or your statement, while you were working on this, did you at any time in the documents that you have studied for this, did you come -- did you encounter a fact that when this objective was defined, was there anything that was ever said that Sarajevo should be completely levelled to the ground?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, this was never something that was --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object. Leading -- leading the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, there is certainly a leading element in that question. I have, however, a different problem; that is, you ask a lot of questions about matters of which I find no direct basis. For example, these objectives and what was meant for Sarajevo. Could you please indicate to me where I found the basis for that in the statement of the expert. I happen to know something about objectives on the basis of the report of Macedonia, but I don't know whether this is the basis you would like me to rely upon. But could you please tell me exactly where I find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the foundation for these questions can be found in the expert report and the findings that the Prosecution handed over to us and all the documents that were entered into evidence by our learned colleagues when Mr. Robert Donia testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was -- but this report is not an answer to Dr. Donia, as far as I can see, because it deals with substantially different matters, compared to the report of Dr. Donia. So could you please indicate to me where I find in this report the basis, as far as the facts are concerned, because we are talking about objectives and -- let me just look.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my questions that I'm asking the professor to answer, they are as part of the questions that are not specifically included in the statement of the professor. But bearing in mind that we are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just ask you one thing to make it more concrete: You are talking about the decision of the 12th of May. I would say that the report does neither deal specifically with that decision. The witness is answering questions about objectives, part of that decision. I think there were -- you mentioned six, or the witness mentioned six. I've got no idea. It's not in the report. Could you please indicate to me where the report specifically deals with events in May 1992 and later. And I'm -- and where, for example, a basis for the decision of the 12th of May could be found in this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, specifically I said that the professor in his expert report doesn't specifically talk about the decision of the assembly of the 12th of May, but the professor told us about the work of assembly organs, the assembly being the highest legislative body. And as part of professor's answer, considering that he was answering a question on the work of the assembly as the highest legislative body in Bosnia-Herzegovina, he's also spoken about the work of the Assembly of the Serbian People. And in his answer -- because of his answer, a question I had to ask was whether he was aware of the decision of the 12th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. From his answers, I take it that he was aware of it. But -- well, please proceed, but keep in mind that for the Chamber in order to understand the testimony of this expert witness having thoroughly studied his report, it's -- if you enter areas which are -- of course everything is related to everything, but if you go away from the report too far, then the basis for our understanding of the testimony might not be sufficient. But then please proceed. But keep this in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, bearing in mind what you've told us, my question would be: You told us the referendum was called in Bosnia-Herzegovina and that it was not legitimate and that it was on the basis of that not legitimate referendum that a series of decisions were made that were unconstitutional and illegitimate. Do you think that there was inevitable for Bosnia-Herzegovina to be divided along ethnic lines?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: This is something that was foreshadowed earlier. In my report, I did not quote a famous so-called agreement by Adil Zulfikarpasic, who was the number two person in the Party of Democratic Action and later on he was person number one in the Bosniak Muslim organisation. This is an agreement that he tried to have both with Radovan Karadzic and Slobodan Milosevic in the name of Alija Izetbegovic. This happened in the summer of 1991. However, what was much more important was the attempts of the European Union through their famous diplomat Jose Cutilheiro, to try and apply the -- implement the so-called Cutilheiro plan with the presence of the -- an agreement of all three legitimate representatives, that is, Serbs, Croats, and Muslims, that he organises this in such a way that each people would have their own autonomous federal unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, my -- my co-counsel will ask you more specific --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please slow down, Ms. Pilipovic. And you, Professor Cavoski, could you also please speak a bit slower because the interpreters really have difficulties in translating what you're saying. And we'd like to hear it. Let me just look on the screen. Yes. It's also the transcriber, it's not just the interpreters. Perhaps, Ms. Pilipovic, we could ask the witness to resume his answer where he said, "However, what was much more important was the attempts of the European Union," and then the witness came to the Cutilheiro plan. Could you please resume your answer from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. So the European Union through their diplomat, a Portuguese man, Jose Cutilheiro, attempted to implement in practical terms their own plan in Bosnia-Herzegovina or his plan, which provided for Bosnia with the legitimate agreement of all the three constitutive peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina that Bosnia-Herzegovina should be separated into three autonomous units, Serbian, Croat, and Muslim, and that this would be the way to resolve the national question. The Serbs were already to accept this solution, that is, that they Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. would forfeit their right to unite with Serbia, providing that in the future Bosnia they would have a status of constitutive people and their own autonomous unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, another couple of questions that I will ask. Can you tell us, you as an expert constitutional law, can you tell us who was able to interpret the assembly decisions?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: The assembly is a legislative organ, and their decisions can only be interested by the assembly as such. It was from the French revolution, there is such an institution called the "refere legislatif," that is, when there is a dilemma in terms of the meaning of a decision of a legislative body, then this is the institution to which a question is addressed. In the Yugoslav constitutional law, there was such an institution of authentic interpretation. What that meant is that if there was a conflict about the meaning and the range of a particular provision in the law, of a word, of a term in a decision or resolution, then the assembly itself can give an interpretation. If individual deputies do this or anyone else, then this is unacceptable. It's considered as unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So from this answer, we also got your interpretation about what happens when individuals interpret assembly decisions. And you believe this is unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: An individual doesn't have the authority to interpret by himself the meaning and the range or the scope of a decision made by the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: One more question: The decisions adopted by the assembly or issued by the Assembly of the Serb People that we have discussed -- were they binding for the army --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the answer -- could the answer please be repeated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your last answer. You said: "An individual doesn't have the authority to interpret by himself the meaning and the range or the scope of a decision made by the assembly." Was that your whole answer or did you -- yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I said -- what I said is an individual doesn't have the authority to do that by himself. As a lawyer, I believe that only an assembly can do that or courts. And courts are the ones that are the masters of the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have finished my part, and I believe that we have another 30 minutes. My co-counsel will continue with the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed. I think you started at -- you took approximately 45 minutes until now, a little bit less.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, first of all, I'd like to start from the beginning. And I don't think that I have seen it in the transcript. Could you please confirm -- could you please confirm this expert report that you have compiled and signed.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, of course. Of course. That's why I've come. I've come to confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Indeed. But I just wanted this to be done formally for the transcript. Now, Professor, let us go back to the aspect of the Cutilheiro project. First of all, can you give us a time frame, please.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I have already said that before this project there was an initiative by Adil Zulfikarpasic, he was, first of all, the man number two in the SDA party. And later on he was the president of the Bosniak Muslim organisation. For a long time he lived in Zurich, that is, he lived in Europe. And it was very shrewdly that he concluded that in fact Muslims have been living with Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the largest number of municipalities and that, therefore, the interest for the Muslims -- life interest for the Muslims, that it was the most important for the Muslims to find a suitable agreement with the Serbs rather than going with the Croats against the Serbs. And it was then that with the agreement -- that is what he says in his memoirs -- that with the agreement of Alija Izetbegovic, he came to Belgrade. And there he spoke to Radovan Karadzic and Slobodan Milosevic. And he was, as he said then publicly -- he was just about to conclude this historical agreement. But this failed because Alija Izetbegovic kept thinking that he would be able to achieve full independence of a unified Bosnia-Herzegovina, and because of that he frequently went to the Libyan Dzamahirija and sent his representatives to the fundamentalist Iran. And then came the second stage --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor, I'm going to have to stop you here. We'll come back to the second stage. We'll come back to the second stage. But before that what I wanted you to clarify or to give us a precision of this period -- you told us this was before the Cutilheiro plan, but what was the period, what was the month, what was the year, and so on?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: That was May or June 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What's your objection, Ms. Mahindaratne?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No. I just mentioned that there was no interpretation for a moment. It's just that the wire has come off. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then if interpretation is restored, please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: After this interruption, I will proceed. What I am interested in is to find out - and I believe that it is clear in the transcript - when was this? Very well. Now, between this period, that is, May or June 1991, and the implementation or the start of the Cutilheiro plan, what was happening in the political life in and around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: When we are speaking about the political life, it was Lord Carrington who influenced it greatly. He had some ideas about a special status, so-called. He was thinking about the special status of Serbs in the Republic of Croatia, and most probably for the Alb Aras people, the Albanian people in Kosovo and Metohija, and also for the Serbs -- or Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And Alija Izetbegovic, that says in my report, it was because of this he said that he completely agreed with this and saying that the Serb people had a right to a special status which would mean to be autonomous, to have an autonomous unit of the Serbs within Bosnia-Herzegovina. So as you can see, this whole time there was this idea in the air that Bosnia-Herzegovina must be divided into three autonomous units, and therefore, Sarajevo as well. As I said, Sarajevo had ten municipalities. So there were Serbian municipalities there as well, and there was also a plan to think about creation of Serb Sarajevo within this autonomous unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You spoke to us about Alija Izetbegovic. And my question in relation to that is: Have you ever in all your academic history, have you ever supported Mr. Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I knew Mr. Alija Izetbegovic personally. He was imprisoned because of the so-called Islamic declaration. And a committee which was chaired by Dobrica Cosic, and I was its secretary and member, and we took him to -- wanted to defend him. And at the time Alija Izetbegovic wrote to us and to me from prison, which at the time was completely forbidden. We used to see each other, and I believe that the last time we saw each other, that was prior to the establishment of the SDA party in Sarajevo when I was in the company with him and Adil Zulfikarpasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. But how did you react when he was called to your location?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, that was in the 1980s, and at the time we formed a committee -- we were a committee who defended people who were victims because of their opinions. When we defended people who had said something or written something and then suffered the consequences because of an article -- notorious -- Article 118, we would then defend their right to speak up and to write, which doesn't mean that we identified ourselves with the positions they expressed. At the time I was critical of the Islamic declaration, but I thought that Izetbegovic had the right to say in public what he thought, regardless of the fact that it wasn't necessary for me to agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes. If I have understood you well, Professor, you're telling us that you reacted as an intellectual in accordance with Voltaire's statement, it was in order to defend a principle, the principle of free speech, which can be expressed regardless of which form it takes. Is that how I am to take your testimony?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. And we defended everyone, not just Serbs but let's say Dobroslav Paraga as well, and a number of Muslims, Omer Behmen, Hasan Cengic. Hasan Cengic was later the deputy and the Minister of Defence in the course of the war. Some Albanians too. That was quite simply our position.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I now want to go back to your chain of reasoning. You spoke about this idea which was in the air which concerned the structure of the State of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I would appreciate it if you could now go into more details and tell us what the Muslim party -- the strongest Muslim party could have done at the time during this period and with regard to this idea. Did you present -- did they want to present this idea? Did they want to fight against it? Et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: The position of the SDA, the Party of Democratic Action, with regard to the autonomous constitution of the people within Bosnia-Herzegovina was ambiguous. Alija Izetbegovic and those surrounding him felt that they had to make such a concession. And on this basis, they not only negotiated but they also signed the appropriate agreements according to which such a division of Bosnia into autonomous units was supposed to happen. At the same time, they did everything in their power to abandon such an intention and to betray the people they negotiated with. They did this either by relying on powerful Muslim countries throughout the world, Libya and Iran above all, and they attempted to see certain differences in the positions of EU countries, on the one hand, and the positions of the USA on the other hand. And it appears that the key person who prevented the implementation of Cutilheiro's plan that had almost been finished, it appear that is it was Warren Zimmerman, who was the ambassador of the USA in Belgrade at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor, I apologise. I'm going to stop you there because we haven't gone back to the Cutilheiro plan yet. You mentioned the attitude of the Muslim forces at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And you said they wanted to --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: There was no reference to Muslim forces. The witness has been speaking about the SDA, the political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President. Mr. President, when I say "Muslim forces," I didn't mean the armed Muslim forces. I meant the intellectual sphere, et cetera. I think that everyone understood that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor, a minute ago you spoke to us about the fact that these forces that I mentioned a minute ago would rely on countries throughout the world, on Iran and elsewhere. I would like you to give us further details about this matter, not only about these facts but also about the reality. How did this manifest itself, et cetera, et cetera? Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This line of questioning is going completely -- entirely out of the report submitted by this expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I'll allow you to put this question to the witness, and I'll allow the witness to answer the question. But, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, what I previously said to Ms. Pilipovic is valid for you as well. If you're going into all kind of details on who asked for the support of whom, who went to South America, Australia, Asia, Africa in order to find support, and if we find nothing about these exercises in the report, then of course the Chamber will have to consider that the Prosecution could not be aware of this questioning and that the possibilities of verifying whatever the expert witness says and the transparency which is of major importance for the Chamber might not be observed in the way the Chamber would like it to be observed. So would you please keep that in mind when you continue your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to add that my question didn't have to do with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please ask your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- with people carrying luggage, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, could you please provide more details about these -- the political support obtained throughout the world. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, contrary to Franjo Tudjman and the Slovenian president at the time who -- who mostly visited European centres while Milosevic remained in Belgrade, Izetbegovic turned to the Arab and Islam -- Islamic world. As I have already said, he went to Libya on several occasions, and his people went to Iran quite often. This was quite natural because many people who were clerics, Imams, and hodzas, they were educated in Cairo. That was most often the case -- or in Iran or in Baghdad, some other Muslim or Arab country. They could speak the Arabic language because the Koran is in Arabic, so it's necessary to know it. And thus, they would travel to those countries seeking the necessary support.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to focus on the plan itself, Cutilheiro's plan, which was aborted. First of all, could you confirm what happened as far as the first plan is concerned, the first time it was signed.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: The first plan, the so-called historical agreement which fell through - I didn't even mention it - it fell through because Alija Izetbegovic withdrew from that and he left Adil Zulfikarpasic, he left him alone. He betrayed him. So Adil Zulfikarpasic it turned out negotiated without any authority with Slobodan Milosevic and with Radovan Karadzic, and he was very much affected by this and since that time he no longer played a key role in public life in Sarajevo and in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. What can you tell us, if you know anything about this, about what Mr. Alija Izetbegovic said when an agreement was finally reached between the three parties concerned?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I've already mentioned this, that after a conference that was held in Brussels and where this plan by Carrington -- Lord Carrington was presented on the special status, Alija Izetbegovic on that occasion said, and this is in my report -- Alija Izetbegovic said that he would recognise, he would accept any Serbian request for Serbs to establish their own autonomous units, and he said that he considered this legitimate. But when the European Union engaged the Portuguese diplomat Jose Cutilheiro to negotiate with all three sides, Alija Izetbegovic participated in this himself and he signed that plan too. I can also discuss the details of that plan later on, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I would be very grateful if you could tell us very briefly what happened after the signing of this agreement.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: When this plan was signed, it in fact established certain constitutional preconditions, certain constitutional principles, as they were called that had to do with the new constitutional organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Each of the three constituent peoples was to have its own federal unit or its own autonomous unit, and the division of Bosnia into three units had already commenced, and a principle had been established according to which when petitioning BH, the population census from 1971, 1981, and 1991 should be used, and it already had been established which municipalities were not in dispute, which municipalities would be Muslim, Croat, or Serbian, and that this would not be disputed. And there was a list of municipalities which were still in dispute as to whether they should be Croat, Muslim, or Serb. And then it was a matter of whether these municipalities should join a certain unit or whether certain municipalities, individual municipalities, should actually be divided.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you there, Professor. You will continue in a minute. But with regard to this list of municipalities, did this concern many municipalities or was it an obstacle that one might consider to be a minor obstacle? What can you say about this? And then you can carry on with your presentation.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, according to the way it was presented in the press, it was an obstacle that could have been overcome, for sure. So one expected this work to be carried out. All three sides were expected to make concessions. No one would be totally satisfied -- no one would be able to achieve its objective in full, but it would have to make certain concessions so that the other side could obtain certain things. And in return, concessions would be made to the side that had already been concessions. I think that this procedure could have been completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. So as a result, what happened then, since this did not occur? Can you tell us about it?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, in Sarajevo, Cutilheiro's plan had already been signed. There was -- it was ceremoniously declared, and the representatives of all three peoples had to meet -- were to meet in Lisbon. Then the American ambassador, Warren Zimmerman, came to Sarajevo to talk among other things to Alija Izetbegovic as well. We don't have reliable information about what was discussed, especially since Warren Zimmerman, according to what we can read in the literature, interpreted the contents of his discussion in various ways. It appears that on that occasion Alija Izetbegovic complained and said that, well, he had to accept a plan that he was not happy with. And Warren Zimmerman then told him, "Well, why should you accept it?" And Alija took this to mean that it wasn't necessary to accept it. He thought this was a diplomatic way of saying it wasn't necessary to accept it, and he thought that America would support the independence of Bosnia even if Alija Izetbegovic rejected this plan that had almost been completed, this EU plan that had almost been completed. In my opinion, this was the casus belli, the cause of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor, thank you. A minute ago you told us about the ten municipalities that formed Sarajevo. You spoke about relative majorities in these municipalities. My question is as follows: As far as the country, the so-called rural zones are concerned, and as a general rule, how were the majorities divided in ethnic terms in these areas? What was the ethnic composition in these areas?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I'd just like to clarify something about the status of the city of Sarajevo and the status of the municipalities. These municipalities were normal municipalities. They resembled all other municipalities. And then the town of Sarajevo as a superstructure covering these municipalities had a twofold responsibility. One was to transfer the responsibility of those municipalities to the town and the second part of its responsibility had to do with what the republic transferred to the town. So one could freely say that this concerned ten municipalities. In historical terms in Bosnia, first of all the Turks and then the Muslims mostly lived in towns because they weren't involved in agriculture or in livestock. They were agas or beys. They had state professions, they were judges or tradesmen, et cetera. So they mostly lived in urban areas. There were some exceptions, along the River Drina -- along the estuary of the River Drina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps you could slowly repeat the two names that you mentioned a minute ago just for the sake of the transcript so that the matter is clear. They were --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, they were agas and beys. These are feudal terms. And then they were kadijas, these are judges. And then they held other professions, for example they were Imams or hodzas. These people were clerics. There were many other professions. Naturally I can't remember all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Professor, let us now return to the political majority of the Muslims in relation to the possible acceptance of a plan such as the one presented by the diplomat Cutilheiro. According to what you know - and I'm not talking about Alija Izetbegovic himself - but did the Muslim party or the majority of the Muslim party desire this plan to be accepted, or did they want it to be rejected?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Unfortunately I'm not in a position to answer that because at the time there was no serious research of public opinion. That was a period that preceded the war. So the party leaders decided for their people about the fate of their people and about the fate of Yugoslavia and about the fate of Bosnia and Herzegovina. If people had been aware of the fact that war was terrible - and it really was terrible - they would probably all have accepted Cutilheiro's plan and then the war in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina wouldn't have happened. But someone thought that it was possible for the state to secede and that it was possible for a constituent people to be deprived of its right to enjoy the status of equality without this leading to war. As far as I know - and I have studied constitutional law - secession, which is unconstitutional, is usually carried out by having recourse to war, and it leads to war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor, let's now have a look at the other side, please, the Serb side. According to the research that you have carried out, were you able to determine whether the Serbian side - and we're talking about the period of February, spring 1992 - at that time did the Serbian side support the implementation of this plan or the implementation of a similar plan?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: As far as the Serbs are concerned, in Bosnia and Herzegovina and in Croatia, above all, their natural tendency was to preserve the integrity of Yugoslavia or to remain at least within the framework of a rump Yugoslavia. So if someone wanted to secede, it shouldn't be possible for the secession to be carried out if it concerned territory where the Serbs were in a majority. This was the first objective of the Serbs. The Bosnian Serbs, who were led by Radovan Karadzic, the Serbian Democratic Party, went one step further and made more significant concessions that could have damaged the Serbs in Croatia, in historical terms. When the SDS accepted Cutilheiro's plan at a given moment, it in fact rejected the possibility of joining Serbia, of being unified with Serbia. It accepted Bosnia as a possible future independent state under the condition that the Serbs in such a Bosnia should have their own autonomous federal unit. I know that the current Bosnian leaders reluctantly said that they were prepared for such a sacrifice in order to avoid a war, although it was obviously a better option to preserve Yugoslavia and to ensure that all Serbs were in one state, as they were since 1918.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor, thank you. And since Sarajevo is a key problem, given the majority that the population had in Sarajevo, did the administrative partition of the city -- could the administrative partition of the city have been done, been carried out, at a lesser cost; that is to say, without the loss of life, et cetera, which is what happened later on? Could the administrative partition have been achieved without paying such a price?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes, obviously. I said that in the central municipalities the Muslims had a significant majority. But in the border municipalities, which were in the suburban parts of the town or had earlier on been the rural parts of the town, the Serbs were in the majority there. Naturally these municipalities had fewer inhabitants, were not as densely inhabited. So such a partition could have been accepted, depending on which people had the majority, or some other sort of partition could have been accepted given the appropriate concessions. But this would have enabled the war -- this would have enabled us to avoid the war. But since someone desired -- from the time that someone desired the entire city of Sarajevo, it was no longer possible to avoid the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You said "someone." Are you referring to anyone in particular?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I'm thinking of the Party of Democratic Action, the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, I am thinking of Alija Izetbegovic and the other people who led that party.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, a minute ago you mentioned the intervention in diplomatic terms of the American ambassador, and you mentioned the reaction that followed. Could you expand on that, on this aspect of the problem.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, that reaction was -- was a bad reaction, and it led to war. Alija Izetbegovic was given a silent promise according to which Bosnia and Herzegovina, even without Cutilheiro's plan, would be internationally recognised. And even before he managed to obtain international recognition, his government, the rump government, naturally without the Serbs - I think it was on the 4th of April - his government declared a general mobilisation and thus made it known to everyone that it would use certain means if war broke out, if there was a conflict. I didn't discuss this. I'm not a military expert, and this doesn't fall within the domain of constitutional law. But I know this because I followed the papers. I know that the Muslims established the necessary paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor, you're not a military expert. A minute ago you used the term "casus belli." I'd appreciate it if you could tell us why in your opinion this chain of events couldn't have been interpreted in your opinion by the other party as anything other than a casus belli.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: In my report, and I think it's quite clear, the balance between the three peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina was a very delicate one, and it was very dangerous if one of the peoples was oppressed, because two of the peoples had joined and were against it or because one of the peoples was in charge of the situation. Only full equality and respect for the state-forming nature of the state and the constituent character of the peoples, only such respect could ensure peace among the citizens. When the SDA, the Party of Democratic Action thought that it could obtain international recognition of a unified Bosnia and that it could reduce the Serbs to the status of the -- to the humiliating status of an ethnic minority, they should have been aware of the fact that this represented a casus belli.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have another two questions. Would you like me to ask them now or after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you could finish in a couple of minutes, I'd like you to continue your questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor, my penultimate question will be as follows: According to your experience and your research, do you think that Europe, given what it knew - and I'm talking about the historical and political Europe- do you think that they could have expected -- they could have foreseen such an event?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, it was very easy to foresee it. In 1847 six Swiss cantons formed the Zonderbund alliance and tried to secede. This was followed by the well-known Zonderbund Krieg or Zonderbund war. And it wasn't until '48 that the current constitution of Switzerland was adopted, which was the constitution of the federal state. Although, Switzerland is still nominally a confederation. In 1861, 13 southern states in the USA left the union, formed a confederative alliance, and armed its militia, and the constitution allowed for this -- the federal constitution allowed for this. But when the militia in South Carolina attacked a fortress, this was a casus belli. As you can see, secession always leads to war. I can also mention the case of Biafra. This is a more recent event. The Biafra case in Africa secession. The succession of a federal unit which is unconstitutional leads to war. Today we are still facing the consequences of the Chechnia problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor, my very last question: It won't interest Nicolas de Flue but it has to do with reasons of credibility. Who is comrade Tacitus and what can you tell us about this, the Tacitus comrade?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Tacitus.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Tacitus. The -- I think you are referring to the criminal offence that I committed in 1972 according to the findings of the court. In the work on the value of Yugoslav law, I quoted Tacitus and his annals, and in particular the well-known phrase "corruptissime respublica plurime legis," which means the more corrupt a state is, the more laws there are. So the court in Tito's Yugoslavia at the time thought that this was the dissemination of false information. And because of that quote, because of the quote from Tacitus' annals, I was sentenced to five years in prison and I was given a two-year conditional sentence -- two-year suspended sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions. I thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until twenty minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, is the Prosecution ready to cross-examine the expert witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as he enters the courtroom, you may proceed. Professor Cavoski, you'll now be examined by counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, professor.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: [In English] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, according to your curriculum vitae, which you have provided with your report, your academic qualifications and professional experiences are all exclusively in the field of law, in the legal field; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not quite the case. I am also working on political philosophy. I think you are able to see that with a colleague of mine I co-wrote a book on Esquilus, on his arrest. That is a tragedy written by the most famous tragic playwright of all times who lived in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. fifth century, BC. Then together with Vojislav Kostunica, who is currently the federal president of Yugoslavia, I published a book in history, that is, "Political pluralism or monism." So I worked on different things apart from those that are to do with the field of law.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Apart from the publications and what you've just stated, you do not have a degree in history or political sciences?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: No. No. I am a Doctor of Law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as I was adjusting my headphones and I heard the name, I'm not sure -- I didn't hear the name of the author from the fifth century before BC. It doesn't appear in the transcript, so could it be repeated. I believe I'm talking about the playwright, Mr. President. I believe that is Esquilus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the name of the writer you told us about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The author of a Hellenistic study about the ancient Greek playwright, Esquilus who wrote a trilogy called Orestiade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You've repeated the name. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So in view of that, I suggest to you that your report, which relates to the subject of history, should be ideally submitted by a historian is outside your area of expertise since you are a professor of law, to use your own words.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: If you have read my report carefully, you will see that one of the key books that I quoted is a book by Mustafa Imamovic about the state and legal position of Bosnia-Herzegovina dated from 1878 until 1914. You see, this person, Mustafa Imamovic, among other things, he was a colleague of mine at the university. He's one year older than me. During the war he was a dean of the legal -- of the law school in Sarajevo. He completed a law degree, but he dealt with legal history. When legal history is in question, we believe that people who are dealing with this, they should have study in law and then they learn about history. Rather than being historians and then trying to, as historians deal with the history of law. That is far more difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So speaking about your publications, I note in your list of publications there's a notable omission. You omitted to mention one of your publications. You're nodding your head. Do you know what I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Which publication did I not list, if you please? I have listed all the books that I have written.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is it your position, sir, that all the books you've written are listed in your list of publications attached to your curriculum vitae? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, you see, obviously you don't have a list of published works, obviously. With us it's not usual to list a smaller publications between 50 and 100 pages -- or under 50 and 100 pages, particularly if certain publications are published later with other publications in other books. So please, can you just tell me the name of the publication that you're thinking about, what -- so that I can tell you whether it is -- it is included in the book. And if it is not so, then perhaps it's an article which is quite difficult for me to list because that would be over 200 titles.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, you wrote a book by the name of "The Hague against justice revisited." And it is not in your list of publications. What is the reason for this omission?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, there's no reason. It is included in this. Let me expand on this: When the case of General Djordje Djukic came before the Tribunal, I wrote the book "The Hague against justice." Perhaps it should have been "The Hague versus justice."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. You have listed your first book "The Hague against justice," but you have omitted to list a book which has more pages than the first book, so it's certainly not a small publication, which is "The Hague against justice revisited." So could you explain to us how you list one book and not the other?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: First of all, what I've published about General Djordje Djukic, that was, I think, in 1996. After that I published this other book, both in Serbian and in English. But as a small booklet. The first one is also a small booklet. But this is "The Hague against justice revisited." And then after that in Serbian I published ten or so processed cases, and then I've put it all together in one book, also about General Djordje Djukic, about Dr. Radovan Karadzic, and about eight other cases. And then in 1998 in Serbian I published a large study "The Hague against justice," where all previous publications are included in one book.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just allowing myself to say this because sometimes the position of -- sounds important. I don't think that the quote, unquote signs are necessary in line 17, because that's not what the witness said -- no, I didn't say that. Their position, the way that it is -- the way that they are included in the transcript do not reflect the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would say that he didn't express the quotation marks, and he -- when he cites a title of a book, then you think it inappropriate to put that in quotation marks? Is that -- how I have to understood it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I think, Mr. President - but I may be wrong - I believe that the quotation marks could come after the word "justice." And that is not -- it's not -- the title doesn't include this word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just see, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. You are referring to page --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 42, line 15, Mr. President -- page 42, line 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "The Hague against justice revisited." What's wrong with that quotation?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My impression is that the quotation marks should stop after "justice."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just clarify. Did you say that you first wrote a booklet on "The Hague against justice" and that you then wrote a second booklet called "The Hague against justice revisited"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I still do not understand what the problem is, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, I'm referring to -- drawing your attention to your second book, which is "The Hague against justice revisited," which deals with the case of Dr. Radovan Karadzic, and it is described as a line of defence of Dr. Karadzic in a possible ICTY trial that you have written; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: No. No. I simply believed that it was necessary, just like for the case of General Djordje Djukic, that this case should be analysed. And if you did know by any chance the Serbo-Croatian language, you would also be able to see that in a similar way I analysed the cases of, for instance, Dr. Karadzic, Slavko Dokmanovic, the Vuckovic brothers, that is, the Banovic brothers, the case of Simo Drljaca, the case of Goran Lajic, and other cases. So it's been a long time that as a lawyer I have been dealing with these cases that are appearing before this Tribunal, whether they have started or whether they have finished. And I don't think there is anything unusual in that. In fact, it should be expected from experts among the public to carefully follow what this Tribunal is doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. I just ask you one question, whether it was the line of defence of Dr. Karadzic. I put it to you that --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: No, it's not. It's not a defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I put it to you, sir, that you did not specifically mention this second book, "The Hague against justice revisited" for two reasons, first being because it is seen -- and a clear reading of the book shows that it is a line of defence for Dr. Karadzic in a possible ICTY trial. And secondly, because you have referred -- described the Tribunal in extremely negative terms.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I have to say that you are wrong. First of all, people in this field of work know that when a person is speaking about books, these books include works that have at least ten pages. So I decided to just include books that I published. The book that I published here, which is quoted "The Hague against justice," from 1998, where this small piece of work of -- about Radovan Karadzic is included, I did not conceal it except that you thought because I wrote this in English -- I've written the title in original. It was written here in Serbian, so I translated into English. So this work on Dr. Radovan Karadzic, I did not conceal it. I don't know why I would do such a thing. But I don't think that that is -- it's inappropriate for a person, for an expert, to put -- to list smaller works in his list of publications.
