Otherwise, then that seems pretentious, so that's why I put books in my list like "The collection of work," which is from 1998. And I think it's done appropriately, correctly. I didn't put smaller works in. As far as smaller works, I have about 15 of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you did not want to list your smaller works, why did you list your first book "The Hague against justice," which is a very small book?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, it seems that we are not understanding each other. That's not the first book about The Hague. The first book was "The Hague against justice," the case of General Djordje Djukic, and it was published both in Serbian and in English. And it's a small booklet which has 48 pages. What I have listed here from 1998, it's a book which has almost 300 pages. It is a B5 format book.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, do you know someone by the name of Professor Kostunica?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Professor Kostunica, I have known him from early days. And I believe that I met him sometime in 1966 or 1967. From that time we have been friends -- we have socialised together, from the time when we both left the army it was about in 1968 and now --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... due to time restraint, wherever you could answer with a yes or no, please do so.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are you involved with Professor Kostunica in a movement which is referred to as the anti-tribunal movement in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Together with Professor Kostunica, I was a founder member of the democratic party in 1990 -- that is, in 1989. But sometime from September 1990, politically we went into separate ways. For a while we didn't see each other, we didn't speak, so it's been for a long time --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... my question to you is whether you were involved with him or whether you are involved with him in a movement referred to as the anti-tribunal movement in Belgrade. If you can answer with a yes or no, please do so.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: No, no. I do not take part in that with him. No, I'm not involved in that with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And there is such a movement, then.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I don't know that such a movement exists except that what I did - and I can inform you about that - is that as the professor of the law school on two occasions, together with 51 colleagues from the university and there are about 90 lecturers, we submitted a submission to the constitutional court of Yugoslavia where we requested for the constitutional court to start proceedings in order to consider the constitutionality first of one provision of the federal government on cooperation with the ICTY and then in order to check the law on cooperation -- or rather, the constitutionality of a law on cooperation -- on law cooperation with the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, earlier I suggested to you that your reason for not listing "The Hague against justice revisited," that one of the reasons was because you had referred to the Tribunal in extremely negative terms. And did you agree with that or don't you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I have to say that like any critically conscious lawyer, I critically examined its work. And in those publications, I listed a number of critical remarks about this Tribunal, starting from when it was founded and also the way it operated. But I did this just like many other lawyers in the world did and as they will continue to do in the future. This is nothing unusual in law. No one is outside criticism.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, is it your position that the terminology you've used is in a scholarly sense?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I have your book "The Hague against justice revisited" here, sir. And you start with the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Which I will read to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If it's necessary, Mr. President, I have photocopies of the relevant page. Otherwise, I would just read the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would start reading it. If it's not too many -- but perhaps you would give a copy to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Yes, please. And of course, like always, if we can have a copy in Serbian because the authenticity of the text is very important. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have a copy in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. In Serbian -- in Serbian it's printed on one side and in English on the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's how the book is printed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will read the first paragraph to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please listen carefully.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I also get the copy of -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think there's --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You start your book with this paragraph: "It has long been known that a bad beginning is a sure sign that things will continue badly. There is even a valid legal principle that time cannot correct or make --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, could you please tell us what you're reading. I have page 47 in front of me. Where do you start?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's page 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I've got 47 in front of me. That's --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Mr. President. You've got the wrong page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It would be --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will read the next page, also, so it can be retained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll keep 47 for the future.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Page 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It is your first paragraph, and that is page 7: Under the title of "The Hague against justice revisited, the case of Dr. Radovan Karadzic." The first paragraph goes like this: "It has long been known that a bad beginning is a sure sign that things will continue badly. There is even a valid legal principle that time cannot correct or make worthwhile that which from the outset was misconceived. As a famous Serbian jurist, Valtazar Bogisic put it, in the form of a national proverb, "Time never straightened a hunchback." The saying fits the International Tribunal at The Hague to a tee. From the very beginning, it was wrongly conceived and badly constituted and in the course of trying the first cases brought before it, has shown absolutely no sign of improvement." That sir, is your first paragraph, and there are --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: -- several such references. Due to time constraints, I will take you directly to your concluding paragraph, which is on page 47. You refer to another --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to make an objection here because I have read these pages. And if this whole series of questioning is about to say that this is offending the Tribunal, I do not see that the comparison with a popular proverb, and we know what popular proverbs are, I don't think there's anything offensive in that or offending. So I object to this type of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as I understand, Ms. Mahindaratne seeks to establish that this expert witness, because of the content of what he has written, intentionally kept away part of his publications. Whether or not she intends to say that the expert is offending the Tribunal and whether it would be bad to offend the Tribunal is, I think, a totally different thing. But perhaps that develops in that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You're correct, Mr. President. My point is that this publication has been kept out. Mr. President, if this can be dealt with in the absence of the witness, I could respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll ask the expert witness to leave the courtroom for a while, and perhaps he could stay -- stand by so that Ms. Mahindaratne could express herself. I -- unfortunately, but you as a lawyer will understand that sometimes procedural issues have to be discussed. Thank you for your understanding. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the reason for this is threefold. Firstly, Mr. President, the Prosecution intends to demonstrate that through these passages the type of low esteem the witness has for this Tribunal -- there is a question as to his commitment to speak the truth before the very institution he has, if I'm permitted to read the rest of the passages -- he proposes should be disbanded, firstly. Secondly, Mr. President, in keeping this particular publication out of his list of publications where he lists a very similar and in fact a more -- a smaller publication but not this, it is very clear that it's an attempt to conceal this type of -- this particular publication from the attention of the Tribunal, from the attention of your Chamber, Mr. President. Thirdly, Mr. President, through the next few questions I intend to demonstrate the bias of this witness towards one side and the lack of objectivity and lack of impartiality, and therefore his incompetency to be treated as an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, first of all, in the twenty-first century to conceal something, when it's enough to click on the Internet to find anyone's publications, I don't think that's very plausible. Secondly, the right to criticise does exist. There are lawyers as it happens who have criticised this Tribunal. They have done it on their own terms. They have done it with full respect. They were never sanctioned. Far from it for, for having done so. The fact that this person could have thought and written that this Tribunal does not have the qualities required structurally speaking, not for internal reasons, doesn't imply at all that his credibility could be questioned. Otherwise, we can read the complete list of works of someone. We can never finish them. We cannot find out whether this person has written about -- in reference to a proverb or in reference to something else. I don't think that there's anything in here that we can say that this person has a specific opinion on this Tribunal. And even if that is the case, the right of everyone is to have such-and-such an opinion about such-and-such a person or such-and-such an institution. That is a sacred right. This person has paid for having defended his ideas. And at the time, he has paid for having defended people with whose ideas he didn't agree, including Mr. Izetbegovic. I believe this is clear, Mr. President. I don't think I said -- I didn't say "I believe this is clear." I said "his intentions should not be put on trial."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I really don't understand you when you are saying the following: "Through these passages the type of low esteem the witness has for the Tribunal -- there is a question as to his commitment to speak the truth." Could you elaborate on that, because I cannot -- this is not my conclusion. I agree with Mr. Piletta-Zanin. I think that everyone is entitled to think about any institution, including the Tribunal, what he thinks.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: And that -- I cannot conclude that for that reason coming here and giving the testimony under oath he is not speaking the truth. I don't -- I would like you to give me some reasons for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, he takes his oath before an institution he describes as, to use his own terminology -- compares to a hunchback. And he, if Your Honour, you may permit me to read out the next passages, he proposes that this institution in the very strongest of terms -- he proposes that it should be disbanded. My point is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: So what?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My point is, Your Honour, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: So what?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My point is before such a forum he has such a disregard for, if he is taking an oath, it is -- there is -- one can easily disregard -- can easily come here and give -- take an oath without any commitment to really speak the truth. That is my point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. With all due respect, now I rebel here, because this witness has never stated that this Tribunal is to be compared with a hunchback. I believe that one has to be able to read. That's the beginning of things. What we have the text here - and I don't have the French translation, which is a shame - when we say that something is a hunchback, that means it cannot be straightened. It doesn't mean it is a hunchback. The words should not be twisted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do agree. Let's first make one thing perfectly clear. This Chamber, without any restriction, acknowledges the right of everyone to express his feelings, his opinions freely. This Chamber does not consider criticism on the Tribunal as a reason not to tell the truth, just as this Chamber would not consider the way someone is spending funds as a reason not to tell the truth. At length, the Prosecution experts have been questioned about financial involvement in supporting certain funds. One could question to what extent that would substantially assist the Chamber in assessing the credibility, reliability of those expert witnesses. Similarly, one could seriously question to what extent attention drawn to this criticism to the Tribunal would assist the Chamber in assessing the reliability or the credibility of this expert witness. The questions as such, to draw the attention to earlier writings of an expert, are not inadmissible. But let's not spend too much time on it for the reasons I just gave. The -- yes, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I just -- just to indicate that I will now move on to another area in the interests of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I would like to say that for me, at least, what this witness wrote in this book or in another book doesn't affect his credibility at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's clear that -- and that I think -- or the Chamber has expressed that these earlier writings are not of great assistance for -- and perhaps as far as credibility and reliability, every of the Judges will make up his mind. And since you indicated that you'll move on to your next subject, Ms. Mahindaratne, I'll ask the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Cavoski, we'll continue. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, are you or were you at any time senator of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Of course I was. I think that we appointed senators towards 1995, and we were appointed as senators by Mrs. Biljana Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. Just wherever you could answer with a yes or no, I would appreciate it if you would do so.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And are you or were you an official of the Serbian Liberal Party?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I was the president of the main committee of the Serbian liberal party from the time it was founded. That was in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The Serbian Liberal Party is considered as a conservative Serbian political party; isn't that the case, sir?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of its name, you couldn't say that it was conservative. You'd conclude that it was liberal. Otherwise, we would have been called the Serbian Conservative Party. It's necessary to know what words mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well. Sir, do you not think it would have been appropriate to indicate your political involvement that you were a senator and an official of the Serbian Liberal Party in your curriculum vitae which you have provided with your report?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: My political lifespan is very rich. I thought it was necessary to mention only the most essential factors. I was the founder of the democratic party, for example, which is now led by Mr. Zoran Djindjic. I didn't think it was necessary to mention that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are you not a close associate of Dr. Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I am not an associate of Dr. Radovan Karadzic's but I was a friend of his.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you were in the close circle of friends of the former president, Mr. Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: As far as Slobodan Milosevic is concerned, I'd need a little more time to answer that. I started my university studies with him at the same time. I knew him very well. But in 1968, after those well-known student demonstrations, we parted ways. And since that time I was not a political friend of his. And as you could see from my curriculum, in 1991 I published a book. It was called "Slobodan protiv slobode." That is to say, Slobodan against liberty.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, do you know a person by the name of Vojislav Seselj - pardon my pronunciation?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes. I personally know Vojislav Seselj, and I met him when he started having serious difficulties in Sarajevo. At the time he was a lecturer at the faculty of political science.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, due to time restraint, I would appreciate it if you could restrict your answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: He's an author, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that the witness is going to have the leave the courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or I could phrase it -- put it in French if the witness doesn't understand French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... speaks or understands any French.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will take my -- I don't understand French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't understand French. But then, of course, we'll have the problem of Ms. Mahindaratne having to respond in English. So perhaps it's better -- unless -- it's just --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In very general terms, Mr. President. My objection has to do with the fact that when politicians are mentioned who have certain connotations, we can't satisfy ourselves with a yes or no answer. We have to allow the witness to continue so that we are familiar with the context. That's my objection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If the witness needs to explain an answer, then of course he can ask whether he may do so. On the other hand, if the question is just do you know a certain person, then perhaps the next question could already elicit from the witness what he wanted to say. So we'll start -- yes. You may put on your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I proceed, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may put on your headphones.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the witness should first wait and see what the next questions will be. And if then finally something important is missing, then he could explain that. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, would you answer my question, which was -- I was referring to Vojislav Seselj, who was an author. He was an author, isn't he -- or he is an author. He's an author?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Vojislav Seselj is not a great author. We consider him to be a pamphleteer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, haven't you reviewed and recommended his publications and I will give you the titles of some of his publications that you recommended, the person that you don't consider as a great author. One is the publication titled "The campaign against the heretic." Second is "Twilight illusions." Another one is "Democracy and dogma." These are three of his publications that you've recommended.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: The first book is called "Pursuing the heretic." And I read that book and recommended it. And that is a description of his experience in Sarajevo. And then as a friend -- at the time we saw each other, I suggested certain other books until he offended me and I haven't spoken to him for ten years now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is that why you called him -- you said that you don't consider him an author now, but there was a time you considered him as a great author? You've changed because you don't speak to him now, sir?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I'm afraid you have misinterpreted what I said. His first book was a testimony that was very affecting. And as such it had to be published. But as far as the legal field is concerned, and he is a lawyer, his works don't have great value. And this is well known.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it the case that in most of his publications - and I did not at any stage refer to legal publications. I just used the word "author," - in most of his publications he's quoted you or used your articles or refers to your own publications as his source references. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: That was the case in the publications that were published 10, 12, 13 years ago. But in his most recent publications, he says that I'm barking at the moon like someone crazy.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Weren't a number of his --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I apologise, but it's difficult to see the relevance of a question which has to do with whether a person who is not directly or indirectly connected to this case, about what someone said. I don't see the relevance.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm just coming to that, Mr. President, my last point on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Coming to what, Ms. Mahindaratne?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My point of this line of questioning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's then listen to your next question and see.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, weren't quite a number of Mr. Seselj's publications, including the one you recommended, banned by -- in Belgrade by district court as being extremely nationalistic publications and having the capacity to use the terms of the district court judgment, "which could have disturbed the public"?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Naturally those publications were forbidden. But you're taking me back to a terrible period, which I lived through and I never accepted the right of the court to sanction so-called opinions. So regardless of whether we agree with what Vojislav Seselj or someone else says or doesn't say, we have no right to deprive such a person of the right to express his or her position.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, weren't your services terminated by the political science department of the faculty of law of the Belgrade university in 1975 on the basis that you were morally and politically unfit for the job of associate professor, which were the words used by the commission which enquired into your reappointment? Wasn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: That's what it says in the report of that commission. Three of my professors drafted that report. I published that report. In the book "Revolutionary Machiavellianism." But I was dismissed for my opinion. That's what I was condemned for.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In using the terms you were politically unfit, wasn't it the case it was your extremely nationalistic stance that disqualified you from reappointment to the political science department of the faculty of law of the Belgrade university?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: One can tell that you don't know me well or that the information you have about me is not correct. When I was dismissed from the university, no one spoke about me in terms of a nationalist. No one said I was a nationalist. I was dismissed because I had criticised Tito's regime. That was the real reason for which I lost my job. In the communist system, it's not at all unusual for professors to be removed from their university posts.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, I suggest to you that in view of your political involvement and association with the political leadership of Republika Srpska and the Serbian political leadership, as well as your actions in recommending publications which have been banned judicially for being extremely nationalistic, you have demonstrated very clearly that you're extremely biased and you possess extremely nationalistic views?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is not a question. It's a distribution. All I can do is reject it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can I suggest to you, sir, that in view of that clear bias and lack of impartiality on your part you cannot be -- you're not a competent witness to render an opinion on the political history of the conflict of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Naturally that's one of the party's opinion, and it's up to the learned Chamber to assess whether this is the case or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So you would agree then, sir, that your opinion is from the perspective of, to use your own terms, "one of the parties"?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: No. I said that that is your description. You described me as an extremist, a nationalist. That is the opinion of your side. And the Chamber, being impartial, shall decide whether I can be accepted as an expert witness or not. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please move to your next subject, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, in your paper, the central thesis of your report was that war was inevitable, owing solely to three events, being, firstly, the decision of the BH Presidency and government to seek independence, referring to 23rd December, 1991; secondly the Badinter commission's interpretation of nationality rights in January 1992; and thirdly, Izetbegovic's alleged annunciation of the Lisbon agreement in March 1992. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I think that the casus belli is the first item mentioned and the third one, as far as the opinion of the Badinter Commission is concerned, which you mentioned under number 2, well, I just indicated that there were shortcomings in that opinion and I emphasised this, if you were careful enough to read this. And I emphasised the fact that Badinter's Commission abandoned the usual concept of a national minority, and in fact it covered all the peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina with this term. So in fact, there was not a single people that had a majority. And then it spoke about the rights of the Serbs as an ethnic minority.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Well, you explicitly argue that the alleged negation of Bosnian Serb group rights in these -- now, as you say two events then, not taking the second one -- made war inevitable. That's what you say, the casus belli, to use your term.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I'd also like to add that the attempt to secede itself was a casus belli. So if you examine the history of the federal states, the attempts of one or several federal units to secede as a rule result in war.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And less explicitly, you suggest that these events validate and justify the war?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I'm not talking about justifications of war. I'm talking about provocations, provoking war. And there is an important difference to make there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I object about the value of the words, the weight of the words. Once one has asked a witness whether this justifies war -- if one is a lawyer and if one is aware of the weight that words have, then one is saying something that has a lot of importance. And the Defence protests. They can't accept this. As a general rule, war is not justifiable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not engage in a legal debate on whether war could ever be justified or not. This is not the place to enter such a debate. But in more general terms, Ms. Mahindaratne, it does not greatly assist the Chamber, if you first simplify the report of the expert witness, ask him then whether he agrees with your simplified version of his report, and then invite him in this way to report -- to repeat what he's written and what the Chamber has read.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will move on to another area, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, I draw your attention to page 30 of your report. And I have the English translation. Maybe you'd have perhaps the corresponding page to page 30.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes. [In English]

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In the first paragraph, which is the last paragraph before the fourth section starts. And I'm referring to the paragraph which starts with the word "transformation." The last three lines of that paragraph reads in these terms. You say: "They say that he had done so after his talk --" I will read the line before that to bring it into context. "And then, for many, a completely unexpected happened. Alija Izetbegovic treacherously withdrew his signature from the said document and thwarted a successful completion of the conference in Lisbon." And then you go on to say, "They say he had done so after his talk with the American ambassador in Belgrade, Warren Zimmerman, and some even add that it was at the ambassador's suggestion that this life-saving plan failed and a three-year civil war started." Sir, when you say "they say" and "some add", what is your source of information? Who are you referring to here?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: First of all, the source of information were in the press, then various memoirs wars. Warren Zimmerman himself on several occasions provided various versions of that conversation that he had. You can read this in the books on the unfortunate events in Bosnia and Herzegovina. What is certain is that after that conversation with Zimmerman, Alija Izetbegovic withdrew his signature from Cutilheiro's plan that had already been shaped. The details of that conversation haven't been disclosed to date, but this Chamber can request from the American State Department the official report that the ambassador Warren Zimmerman certainly made as ambassador to his country, and then they could check to see what the contents of that conversation were.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, as a person who has written many books and there are many publications to your credit, would you not agree with me that it is not competent scholarly work to refer to abstract entities such as "they" and "some" without giving a proper source reference, especially in a report such as this where you're tendering it for the perusal of judicial body?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I must say you are not right. I'll provide you with an example from history. It's Britannicus' murder, who was the adopted brother of the emperor Neron. He was killed and Tacitus says that he was probably poisoned. But then he adds, some say that he was poisoned; others, that he wasn't. But what we will decide depends on both. It's a question of whether we will ever know what was discussed in that conversation. But it's very likely that Warren Zimmerman managed it one way or another to incite Alija Izetbegovic to withdraw his signature. But what we know for certain is he did withdraw his signature after that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, you say -- you used here the words "but it's very likely that Warren Zimmerman managed it one way or another to incite Alija Izetbegovic to withdraw his signature." How can you conclude this? What is your source of information? What are you basing your conclusions on?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Like I said, I followed the press carefully, and then it's a fact that Warren Zimmerman spoke to him, and it's a fact that Alija Izetbegovic accepted the plan up until that point. And after they had spoken to each other, he withdrew his signature. What more would you like to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, when you say "press," which press are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I'm referring to the press in Sarajevo and in Belgrade. I read Serbo-Croat, which means that I am able to read everything that is published in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you read the New York Times?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I also read the New York Times occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When this rumour about this alleged conversation between Warren Zimmerman and Alija Izetbegovic did get published in the New York Times, are you aware that Mr. Warren Zimmerman published an article in the New York Times denying and placing the correct sequence of events in the newspaper? Did you read that?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: No, I haven't read that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, is it then correct to -- I put it to you then, sir, that your assertions in your report are quite incomplete. You have not gone through the necessary material to arrive at the correct conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to be completely clear about this, may I ask my learned colleague to have a copy of the newspaper in question so that I can see what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It's the New York Times of 30th September 1993. Perhaps a copy may be given to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, could you please go through the article titled "Bosnian about-face." And you will see Mr. Warren Zimmerman's account of the incident.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Well, you haven't read it before, have you?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I haven't read it before, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So when you prepared your report, which is the subject matter here, you have not perused all material relating to that particular incident; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: You have to know that in the next 50 years no one is going to be able to peruse the complete material in order to give a reliable report. What is necessary, you must know this, is to have access to archives and, first of all, to the diplomatic archive of the State Department. So we have to have the original of the instructions given that were sent from Washington to Warren Zimmerman in Belgrade before he spoke to Alija Izetbegovic, and then the subsequent report by him. It is only on the basis of this that we can then establish what Warren Zimmerman really did. In fact, I fully understand this letter by Warren Zimmerman. He's simply on his own behalf in his own -- and on behalf of the US government, he published this letter in order to remove the responsibility, his own personal responsibility and that of the US government, for the commencement of the war in Bosnia, particularly bearing in mind the efforts of the European Union to avoid this war through the implementation of the life-saving Cutilheiro's plan. Now, I have to say that this is probably -- that I would have had a completely the same conclusions had I read this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, could you find a moment rather soon to have the next break.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. Just one more question and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You make an assumption about an article as to why that article has been published by Warren Zimmerman even without having read it. I suggest to you, sir, that you made -- you arrive at conclusions or make assumptions --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is wrong. This is wrong. Mr. President. Mr. President. This is false. The witness said, "I've read this article," and he said it a moment ago. And we cannot now have it said, things that are falsehoods.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. My point was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: With regard to his assumption why Warren Zimmerman has published this article, the witness merely read the article in this courtroom right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you can't say that he didn't read the article if five minutes ago the expert witness has read the article. But I now understand your question to be that how this expert witness could give an interpretation of the reasons why this letter was written where he has testified that he didn't know it before and that he read it only in this courtroom. Is that your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please answer to that question. And could you please phrase your questions more precisely next time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Would you please answer my question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This answer by Warren Zimmerman published in this newspaper, I hadn't read it before. But even if I had read it, this is what I said, I probably would have had the same conclusion because it was a general opinion based on various sources, press articles, that Alija Izetbegovic did this following the conversation he had with Warren Zimmerman, and it is logical that diplomats who have this duty to also defend their own person and also the respect of their state is that obviously they are trying to publish this letter in doing so. But later on, when this 40- or 50-year ban which stops us from looking in the archives, when it's lifted, then it can be found out what happened. But obviously, if you think that I am wrong, you as the Prosecution and as the Trial Chamber, you can ask the State Department to give you the instructions that were given to Warren Zimmerman and also his report that went to the State Department to establish what the truth was, if that is important for these proceedings, for this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: One more question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, one more question then.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So I put it to you, sir, likewise, you arrive at conclusions based on, to use your own words, general opinions and logic.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: There's no question here. You haven't asked me a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I suggested to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that you -- you suggest to the expert witness that he arrives at conclusions based on general opinions and logic and what his response is to that suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please respond to the suggestion put to you by Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is not appropriate for me. I think I have done my work conscientiously. And when people don't have all the documents and as it happens people have different insights. Expert reports can never be completely identical. The only case from history is the so-called Septuaginta, which was the very first translation of the old testimony from Hebrew into ancient Greek. 70 people were doing this translation work, among whom Septuaginta, and when they compared the translation, they were completely identical, which is -- which was the sign of God's intervention. Since we do not have such intervention, obviously we cannot have identical opinions and they differ and for this reason each of our reports has shortcomings. Obviously -- I'm not a perfect reporter, of course this can be criticised -- of course this can be done a lot better. That's why you have so many expert reports and the Trial Chamber, who is supposed to look into this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This is a good time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then adjourn until 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May the witness be escorted into the courtroom again. Ms. Mahindaratne, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, if I may draw your attention to page 28 of your report. In the first paragraph, you refer to 54 municipalities. I will read the sentence to you. You say: "Thus it was said that more than one half of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or to be exact, 54 municipalities would be completely indisputable because they are more than 90 per cent ethnically homogenous." And then you go on to name a few municipalities. Sir, from where did you obtain the information - and I'm referring to the data that 90 per cent -- that in those municipalities, 90 per cent -- more than 90 per cent was ethnically homogenous. What was your source of information?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: This data I received in these additional papers that -- when they were attached to Cutilheiro's plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What papers are you referring to? Could you name them?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: No. I have a vast series of published articles in newspapers. I used to do press clippings, and it was from those articles, from those papers, that I drew my data, all that was published in the press at the time. Which municipality do you contest?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, have you ever had the opportunity to peruse the population census issued by the state office for statistics of Bosnia-Herzegovina for 1991?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When you referred to statistics, especially in a report of this nature, do you not verify the accuracy of them?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, you cannot check everything. Something has to be taken as such if it is being published continuously and no one contests this so occasionally I dabble in history. And then when you take -- sometimes data is taken from other books without quoting the source. I am not somebody who is dealing with statistics or with population, so that I would have to always check the census from 1991 -- 1981 in order to check the accuracy of the data. By this, what I stated here, I wanted to say that there was a minority of municipalities where this issue of partition would be contestable, while in the majority of municipalities it would be incontestable. That was my idea, and I believe that by listing these municipalities, I've shown this. It is possible that one municipality I've listed here should not be there, but at least then you'll have to tell me which one do you mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, one of the interpretations - I don't know which one any more - was also speaking about '71, census from '71 as well, apart from '81 and '91. When I say "one of the interpretations," I don't know whether it was French or Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I did understand that you referred to 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Mahindaratne, would it not be far more efficient to put to the witness where mistakes were made, if there were any.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm about to do that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if it's just one, one could wonder whether that would affect the line of the report in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'm about to do that. May the witness be shown the population census for 1991. Mr. President, I don't have -- I don't have an English translation, but it's only for verification of statistics. I have sufficient copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, no, I was just asking if there was a copy for General Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there is, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, can you identify this document --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I proceed, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, could -- do you know what this document is, which was just shown to you?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It is a copy of the census population which was published by the statistical -- statistics institution -- or state institution for statistics of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Would you please turn to page 14.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Where statistics for Banja Luka is contained.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I can see.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In your report, you refer to Banja Luka as one of the municipalities which has more than 90 per cent -- which is more than 90 per cent ethnically homogenous municipality. Would you please examine the statistics in this document and state as to whether your conclusion in your report is correct with regard to Banja Luka or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps things are clear for everyone, but it would be good if my learned colleague could read the title of this page, to give us a translation, because there is no English document. My learned colleague, could you please read exactly what it actually says on the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the -- Ms. Mahindaratne, could you please try to read the -- at least the different categories which are mentioned. "Muslimani" at least needs no translation, I take it is Muslims. "Srbi" I take it is Serbian. "Hrvati" I take it is Croatian. "Jugosloveni" is I take it are those people who say that they are Yugoslavs. And "Ostali" could the interpreters please tell us what "Ostali" would be?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The rest. It means the rest. Others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The rest. And then we have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Another category which reads -- I'll spell it out, U-K-U-P-N-O. I don't know how to pronounce it. What would that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Total, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Total.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, for Banja Luka the total population is 195.692, according to the 1991 census. And the Muslim -- the population belonging to the Muslim group is 28.558. Under the column referred to as Serb, it's 106.826. And Croatian, 29.026. And it goes on further. So considering these statistics, would you still maintain your position that this is a homogenous municipality?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: In my report, I said that in order to check the population census from 1971, 1981, and from 1992, it is obvious that the Serbs here in this municipality in Banja Luka have a large majority. And I'd also like to point out to the data that there were 23.656 Yugoslavs. According to my information, those who preferred to call themselves Yugoslavs were mostly Serbs. Muslims didn't do this at all, least of all Croats. Of course there were some people from mixed marriages. So yes, I admit that here certainly there are not 90 per cent of Serbs, but you can see that this figure is something that is far above the others. It's practically two-thirds. And as such, it would be incontestable that it should be Serbian municipality within this unit, which would be within Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, would you please turn to page 19, which gives statistics for Bosanska Dubica municipality, which is also a municipality included by you in your report as being over 90 per cent ethnically homogenous. The total population there is 31.606; the Muslim population is 6.440; the Serb population is 21.728; the Croatian, 488; the Yugoslavian, 1.851; and others, 1.099. Would you still maintain your position which is what you asserted in your report, that this is a municipality which can be considered as over 90 per cent homogenous?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Obviously here it's not 90 per cent. But as you can see, apart from 21.728 Serbs, there are also 1.851 Yugoslavs, for whom you can assume that later on they would declare themselves as being Serbs. So from the point of view of this partition, this municipality was also uncontested. So my data of 90 per cent wasn't quoted in order to show that this was done according to the latest population census, but from the point of view of that plan these municipalities would have been uncontested as to whether they should belong to the Serb, Muslim, or the Croatian entity. So it's only from that point of view that I'm talking about these municipalities being uncontested. It was not my intention. I'm not a person who's dealing with population policies -- population politics, but that was not my intention.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, due to time restraint, I'll quickly take you through to your other municipalities which you quoted in this manner incorrectly. Bosanski Novi, at page 23, where the total population is 41.665; Muslim population is 14.040; Serb population is 25.101; and so on. Then on page 24.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The municipality of Bosanski Petrovac. Likewise, total population 15.621; Muslim population, 3.288; Serb population 11.694; and the rest you'll find the statistics there. And if you please turn to page 99 you will see Stolac, total population 18.681; Muslim population 8.101; Serb population 3.917; and Croatian population 6.188. In fact, in that municipality, which is one of the municipalities you cited as being over 90 per cent homogenous, the Serb population is less than the other two ethnic factions. So I put it to you, sir, you have with regard to five municipalities which I've demonstrated here, there are certainly not over 90 per cent homogenous and you've incorrectly cited the statistics in your report. What do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: First of all, I didn't say that Stolac should belong to the Serbs, which is what you're imputing. But it's obvious that it should be Muslim. Secondly, this list that I received, that was from the papers that I got, where all the three sides agreed that these parties were uncontested. That's why I've published this data. It was from the point of view of the negotiating sides, Muslim, Serb, Croats, that these were uncontested. And for the other municipalities, one would have to negotiate to see how this should be resolved. So of course I'm not saying that Stolac should belong to Serbs. God forbid. It should belong to the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, is it your position that you do not verify the accuracy of data in your publications?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I'd like to say something, madam. Those of us who are dealing -- or working with science, we're trying to approach the truth. And Karl Popper, that I quoted in my works is using an expression -- instead of the truth, he's saying verisimilitude. Now, everything that we are trying to achieve in our works, it's more or less approaching the truth, while the truth itself is only in God's hands, so none of us is that perfect to be able to acquire absolute truth. And of course, I thank you for the criticism that you have demonstrated here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So you do agree then, sir, that your paper may contain many inaccuracies due to, as you say, your inability to acquire absolute truth.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say that these are inaccuracies, but this is more or less approaching the truth. And I have to say that I have done this with full professional consciousness, that I have applied myself fully, and I believe that I have achieved a good result. But it's up to the Trial Chamber to decide. But such perfection that you demand for me, no one else can achieve.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, would you please turn to page 22 of your report. And I refer to paragraph 1, where you say, "It proved, however, that such predictions were not even convincing enough for Izetbegovic himself, because only a few days before this statement was made on October 14th, 1991, the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina with the participation only of the representatives of the Muslim and the Croat nationality and without the presence of the Serb nationality in parliament proclaimed the sovereignty of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Sir, are you aware of the complete sequence of events that took place -- although you refer to the date as the 14th of October, this is -- the correct date is the 15th of October. The sequence of events which took place at the assembly sessions on the 15th October 1994 -- I beg your pardon, 1991, which led to the declaration of sovereignty?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: At a memorandum of the Republic of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina on sovereignty, that is, on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina was adopted on October the 14th, 1991. And for this decision was voted by the SDA and the HDZ, there were 142 votes out of 240. That is the correct data.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, as -- I asked you whether you do know the full sequence of events that took place on the -- at the assembly sessions of the 15th October 1991, which led to the declaration of sovereignty. Isn't it the case that once the assembly sessions were adjourned on 15th October 1991 by its president, Momcilo Krajisnik, the SDA and the HDZ delegates reconvened and approved this declaration but before adjournment party president Radovan Karadzic made a fiery speech suggesting that Muslims might disappear as a nation if they insisted on the sovereign declaration? Wasn't that the correct sequence of events?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Of course I can't remember every single detail, but I know for certain that Momcilo Krajisnik, that is, he adjourned the session and then I would say on their own initiative the deputies of the SDA and the HDZ reconvened in order to pass this memorandum, and this was done, as I said, with 142 out of -- in favour out of 240 votes. I also know the contents of the speech made by Radovan Karadzic on that occasion. That was published.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, before 15th October 1991, before the declaration of sovereignty, wasn't there a process referred to as regionalisation employed by the SDS in operation, from April 1991, and it is due to many such actions that the SDA and the HDZ ended up adopting the declaration of sovereignty of 15th October 1991?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: If you have listened to my answers to Defence questions carefully, I have already explained it was precisely the HDZ in the so-called Herceg-Bosna, which is West Herzegovina in fact, and Central Bosnia, they've implemented the association of those municipalities where Croats had a majority. And I had said that the then-constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina allowed for this. And I had already explained how the Serbs did the same with those municipalities where they had a majority. And I've also explained in detail, if you listened to me carefully, that from the legal constitutional point of view this was not regionalisation. Regionalisation is creation of a regional state, which is something in between a federal system and a unified state. This was not regionalisation in this sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, is it your position that the HDZ and the SDS both employed this scheme at the same time, simultaneously? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I think even that the HDZ went ahead with this first. The Croats did it. Because Croatian state was so much better organised and they cared a lot more for their compatriots in Croatia than the Serbs did so in Belgrade itself, so this is something that cannot be contested, that the Croats had organised themselves in a timely fashion and had created the association of their municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Isn't it the SDS that started this process in April 1991 and the HDZ started this process only in August 1991? Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, it all depends which data you have at your disposal. Otherwise, there's no doubt that this was done for the first time by Serbs in Croatia, that is in the Knin Krajina. And there was a lot of pressure for the Knin Krajina to get joined to the Bosnian Krajina, and the Serbian Democratic Party which wanted to respect the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina believed that from a legal constitutional point of view it was not acceptable to have a municipality -- said municipality joining which would then cross over that Bosnian-Herzegovinian border, so in this sense the SDS was loyal to the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, you stated that in examination-in-chief the Serbian autonomous organisations were constitutional and could not be considered as unconstitutional.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are you aware, sir, that the constitutional court of Bosnia-Herzegovina has found this scheme to be unconstitutional? Are you aware of that decision?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: No, I didn't follow that decision. But it wasn't just a matter of the competence of the constitutional court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but it was also a matter of the competence of the federal constitutional court.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you that in your report you have completely left out the -- this particular process you spoke of - I used the term regionalisation process - which you spoke of in examination-in-chief. In your -- in part 3 of your report, which is the political history of the conflict, you completely left this information out. What was the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Which information are you referring to? The decision of the constitutional court?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No. I'm referring to the regionalisation process employed by the SDS during -- from April 1991 onwards. There is no reference whatsoever to it.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, as you see, the main purpose of my work was to demonstrate what the casus belli in Bosnia was. And I am claiming that the so-called regionalisation that you have referred to - but I don't consider that to be regionalisation - I don't consider this to have been the casus belli in Bosnia, and I quite simply thought that this was irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, in arriving at a conclusion on the casus belli, cause for conflict, wasn't it incumbent upon you to examine all political developments without being selective and to enumerate a relevant aspect of the history of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: You're now making a request which one can't quite simply satisfy. If you read books on history very carefully, for example, on very distant events, you'll notice that each generation feels the need to reinterpret history. For example, as far as the French Revolution is concerned, there have been several interpretations and there will surely be even more. You can't ask an author to be totally comprehensive and to take each piece of information that you consider relevant into consideration. So that sea of information, given that mass of data, each author, even if he doesn't admit this, each author has to adopt a standard as to what is important. And when he's selecting his material, he will follow this criteria. I was expected to write a report, about 30 pages, and I did that to the best of my ability and conscientiously. But to request -- to ask that report to be totally complete, that's impossible. You certainly have other reports, and you'll see that in each report certain objections can be raised. That's, I suppose, one of the consequences of human imperfection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, could you look at the clock and --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm about to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do that, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you that in making your case for casus belli you presented diplomatic constitutional developments in a vacuum, omitting crucial political developments on the ground. And therefore, I submit to you, sir, that your report is selective, one-sided, and reflects your political stance. What do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I can only take note of that. But I would like to repeat that I wrote my report as conscientiously as possible and to the best of my ability. I stand behind it. I have always attempted to say what I thought to be the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Just one more question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That concludes cross-examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Mahindaratne. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, is there any need to re-examine the expert?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. But we won't have any questions that have to do with the vacuum.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, a series of questions were put to you in relation to the report that you have in front of you. So that is going to be our starting point. That is the simplest way to proceed. Can you tell us, since we don't have the document in English, can you tell us whether this document that is supposed to express percentages, does this document also deal with the issue of land property with regard to the communes and the municipalities mentioned? Could you go through it, go through the document and tell us about this.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I would just like to add that the people who drew up Cutilheiro's plan had a census not only from the year 1991 that the Prosecutor has referred to, but they also had censuses from 1971 and 1981, and there were certainly differences in these censuses.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'll turn to that but --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: But when you were talking about the cadastral office, cadastral matters, it's certain that the Serbs were in possession of most of the land. And as the cities didn't cover large surfaces and the surrounding villages and suburban areas covered a far larger area, to that extent the percentage of the territory owned was far greater.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: As a result, in Cutilheiro's plan, did they try and weigh up the number of population and the extent of land property with regard to the ethnic groups that the land belonged to?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course. That was taken for granted. And it was even taken for granted that some municipalities would be partitioned, so some parts were to be separated in which the Serbians had a majority and would be attached to the Serbian entity. It was certainly possible to do that with other parts of other municipalities in which Croats or Muslims were in the majority, not only in terms of the number of inhabitants but also in terms of the property that they possessed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. But when weighing up these factors, Professor, this doesn't -- this isn't something that comes out of this sole document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: No. It comes out of all three censuses. And the factors that I have mentioned when talking about cadastral matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. And when you mention your percentage of 90 per cent, your well-known per cent of 90 per cent, is this a percentage we should take in a global sense, that is to say, after taking into consideration these two factors, the number and property owned?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes. That is certainly the case, but I should add that all the three sides in an attempt to show their citizens that this plan was a good one, they presented themselves in the press -- this was published in the press with such qualifications. So all three sides thought that these municipalities which I have mentioned were municipalities which were not in dispute, and this is for the reason which I have already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, this question directly concerns this study. But first of all, I would like you to tell us the following: Do you know whether in 1993 or even in 1992 the parties attempted to discuss other plans, that is to say, to discuss the possibility of reaching a peace agreement?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, from the time that unfortunate war broke out --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This doesn't arise from cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, I'll gladly explain why this arises, but I have to ask our witness to leave the courtroom, to avoid any difficulties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... point at the place where it derives from in the transcript so that we can see even without the witness to leave the courtroom. But since he is on his way already, he is quicker than Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you -- and if we could try to finish today, then we should hurry up rather than slow down. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it's very simple. I didn't want to do it in front of the witness. I couldn't do it. If we have a look at this document, we can see that the date of the document is 1993, and what is more it's December 1993. This is a period during which obviously if one party is discussing a peace agreement, this party is going to try and present reality in a manner that is most favourable to it. That is to say, in historical terms we were more present in a certain area than you were. And as these figures reflect what carried out by one side, the authorities of Sarajevo, the connection is the following one: These figures were provided certainly, but not in favour of the Serbs. That's for sure. It's more likely that they were in favour of the party that published these figures; that is to say, the Muslim party, because they were going to be used in a discussion, as part of a discussion, if there was to be a discussion. And this is what I would like the witness to tell us about. And as the Prosecution examined the witness at length about these figures and the percentages, I think that we have the right to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what you wanted to ask the witness is whether he has any reason to doubt the correctness of the figures. Is that what you are -- I mean, that's what I would say derives from the examination -- the cross-examination. The witness was presented with these figures, and now you're telling us for what reason they might have been manipulated. That's more or less what you tell us. Why not ask the witness whether he has any specific reason to assume that these figures, whether he knows anything about it and whether there's any reason for him not to accept them because of their reliability. That's the issue you wanted to raise. I'll allow you to put that question to the witness because that arises from cross-examination. Not on whether the parties had all kind of other thing, because that is already part of your explanation why the figures are unreliable, and that's leading the question to an answer where the question as such is perfectly admissible but not by suggesting the answer. Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, whilst that's taking place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Might I take advantage of this opportunity to request a minute before we adjourn this evening to raise a matter very briefly in relation to the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to see whether we can finish with the expert witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, given what we were talking about a minute ago, do you have any reason to doubt the absolute reliability of these figures which were published by the authorities in Sarajevo at the end of 1993 -- 93?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: All three sides in Sarajevo came out with this information to persuade the citizens to accept the plan and to demonstrate that the municipalities I have mentioned were not a problem of any kind. And within that context, this information is very valid, especially if you take into account the possession of land, land property relations. I explained why this was the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... that was not the question. The question was: You have been presented with a document containing numbers by the Prosecution. Is there any reason to assume and what would then be that reason to assume that they are not reliable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. The figures in this statistical report, they are correct for certain. What has been photocopied and brought here, yes, that's accurate. There's no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Professor, when you say that what was photocopied is correct, you want to say that the photocopy is correct or do you want to say that the figures are correct? Which is not quite the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed to your next subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll move on to another subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I would now like to state -- to specify what you said a minute ago with regard to Mr. Zoran Djindjic. You said that you were the founder of his party, of the party that he leads now. And my question is the following: First of all, which party is concerned, and is it a nationalist party or even an extremist party?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, it's the democratic party in power now, which was founded in November 1989. The idea arose in a circle of three men, Vojislav Kostunica, Leon Cohen, and myself. At the time Vojislav Kostunica was ill, Leon Cohen abandoned the project, and I with 13 other co-founders among whom was Zoran Djindjic of course, established, founded that party at the beginning of the 1990s. The first session was held and that's how the party was founded.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, but you still haven't answered my question.
